interest: Shows 1933 Japanese ambivalence toward Jewish refugees and scientists, and 1936 inquiries on Japan's state-sponsored scientific education.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.423, categorized under Japanese technical, commercial, and correspondence education) comprises two distinct items dating from 1933–1936. The primary document (pages 1–12) is an extensive analytical memorandum titled 'A touchstone to some Facile Affinities in the Far East (A Gentile\'s View),' written in Peiping in October 1933 and received in Washington in early 1934, assessing the Japan-German Cultural Society\'s reported initiative to invite exiled German Jewish scientists, scholars, and artists to Japan; it critically examines Japanese geopolitical motives, the rise of domestic militarism, anti-communist paranoia, attitudes toward Russian Jews in Harbin and the League of Nations, and racial discrimination under the Nazi regime. The second item (pages 13–15) consists of January–February 1936 correspondence between Canadian researcher A. E. Corrigan of Ottawa and Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, concerning Corrigan\'s request for State Department data on Japanese university research, leadership training, and state-sponsored national scholarships for a forthcoming book, to which Hornbeck replies suggesting Japanese government yearbooks and diplomatic legations.

subfiles.about: An extensive analytical memorandum evaluating Japanese proposals to offer refuge to exiled German Jewish scholars, placed in the context of Japanese militarism, anti-communist prejudice, and continental expansion.
subfiles.summary: Written in Peiping in October 1933, this memorandum examines announcements by Dr. Naruhiko Sata of the Japan-German Cultural Society inviting distinguished German Jewish scientists, scholars, and musicians ousted by the Nazi regime to take up positions in Japan. The author analyzes the mixed motivations behind the initiative, concluding that Japanese interest stemmed less from pure humanitarian altruism than from utilitarian needs for technological expertise to aid expansion in Manchuria, alongside a shared resentment of Western racial superiority. The paper surveys Japanese suspicions toward Russian Jews in Harbin, media hostility directed at Jewish officials of the League of Nations such as Robert Haas and Ludwik Rajchman, and the ascendancy of military authoritarianism in Japan. Concluding endnotes address the historical aid of American Jewish financiers during the Russo-Japanese War and report instances of Nazi racial violence against Japanese nationals in Berlin.
